items.stem: With the patient supine and the knee flexed to roughly 20-30°, the examiner stabilises the femur with one hand and draws the tibia anteriorly with the other, feeling for the quality of the end point. Which test is this?
options: Lachman test
Anterior drawer test
Pivot shift test
Posterior sag sign
items.explanation: The Lachman is performed at 20-30° of flexion, unlike the anterior drawer at 90°. What you are grading is not just translation but the END POINT: a soft or absent end point is the finding, and it is why the test survives even when the patient is guarding. The lower flexion angle also relaxes the hamstrings, which is a large part of why it outperforms the anterior drawer in acute knees.
items.pearl: Lachman at 20-30°, anterior drawer at 90°. If you are testing at 90° in a swollen acute knee, hamstring guarding will hide the tear.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. Clinical diagnosis of an anterior cruciate ligament rupture: a meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288.

items.stem: A patient stands on the affected leg with the knee flexed to about 20°, holding the examiner's hands, and rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. Which test is being performed?
options: Thessaly test
McMurray test
Apley grind test
Bounce home test
items.explanation: The Thessaly test is a weight-bearing rotation test at about 20° of flexion; a positive is joint-line discomfort or a sense of locking or catching. Its appeal is that it loads the meniscus in a functional, weight-bearing position rather than passively. Its accuracy in independent studies has been considerably less impressive than the original report.
items.citation: Smith BE, Thacker D, Crewesmith A, Hall M. Special tests for assessing meniscal tears within the knee: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evid Based Med. 2015;20(3):88-97.

items.stem: A 24-year-old runner reports anterior knee pain. Which reported feature points toward PATELLOFEMORAL PAIN rather than a meniscal tear?
options: Pain on prolonged sitting, stairs, and squatting, with no history of a twisting injury or true locking
A twisting injury followed by delayed swelling over 24 hours
Intermittent true locking that the patient has to manoeuvre out of
Well-localised joint-line pain reproduced by deep flexion and rotation
items.explanation: Patellofemoral pain is typically insidious, diffuse or peri-patellar, and provoked by loaded knee flexion — stairs, squatting, running, and prolonged sitting (the so-called theatre sign). Meniscal pathology more often follows a twisting mechanism, produces joint-line pain, and may cause true mechanical locking. Note that 'giving way' is unhelpfully non-specific: it happens in both, and in ACL deficiency.
items.pearl: Ask about prolonged sitting. Anterior knee pain that hates sitting still is far more patellofemoral than meniscal.
items.citation: Willy RW, Hoglund LT, Barton CJ, et al. Patellofemoral pain: clinical practice guidelines linked to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2019;49(9):CPG1-CPG95.

items.stem: The examiner strokes upward along the medial side of the knee to empty the medial gutter, then strokes down the lateral side and watches the medial side for a returning bulge of fluid. What is being assessed?
options: A small joint effusion (sweep or stroke test)
Patellar tendon integrity
Medial collateral ligament laxity
A Baker's cyst
items.explanation: This is the sweep (stroke, or wipe) test for effusion, and it detects smaller effusions than the patellar tap, which needs a substantial amount of fluid to float the patella. Effusion matters diagnostically: an effusion appearing within hours of trauma suggests haemarthrosis and raises the probability of ACL rupture, fracture, or patellar dislocation, whereas slower swelling over a day or more is more typical of meniscal injury.
items.pearl: Timing of swelling is a history question worth more than most special tests. Immediate = blood; overnight = effusion.
items.citation: Sturgill LP, Snyder-Mackler L, Manal TJ, Axe MJ. Interrater reliability of a clinical scale to assess knee joint effusion. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2009;39(12):845-849.

items.stem: Order the steps for performing the Lachman test.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine with the limb relaxed and explain what you will do
Support the knee in about 20-30° of flexion with slight external tibial rotation
Stabilise the femur with the outer hand and grasp the proximal tibia with the inner hand
Draw the tibia anteriorly with a brisk, controlled force
Grade the amount of translation AND the quality of the end point, comparing with the other knee
items.explanation: Relaxation is the whole game — a guarding hamstring can mask a complete rupture, which is why the unaffected side is tested first in practice and why the knee is supported rather than held rigidly. The end point matters as much as the excursion: a torn ACL classically gives increased translation with a soft or mushy end feel.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288 (test description and pooled accuracy).

items.stem: Order the steps of the McMurray test for a medial meniscal tear.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine and fully flex the hip and knee
Grasp the heel with one hand and palpate the medial joint line with the other
Externally rotate the tibia and apply a valgus force
Extend the knee smoothly while maintaining rotation and valgus
Record a positive only if a palpable or audible click occurs WITH the patient's familiar joint-line pain
items.explanation: The positive criterion is what most examiners get wrong. A click alone is common in asymptomatic knees; the finding that carries any diagnostic weight is a click or thud accompanied by the patient's familiar pain at the joint line. For the lateral meniscus the rotation and force are reversed (internal rotation with varus).
items.pearl: Painless clicks are noise. Record what the patient felt, not just what you heard.
items.citation: Smith BE, Thacker D, Crewesmith A, Hall M. Special tests for assessing meniscal tears within the knee: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evid Based Med. 2015;20(3):88-97 (accuracy); test description per Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 6th ed. Elsevier Saunders; 2014.

items.stem: Order the steps for goniometric measurement of knee flexion.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine with the hip and knee in neutral extension
Centre the goniometer fulcrum over the lateral epicondyle of the femur
Align the stationary arm with the greater trochanter and the moving arm with the lateral malleolus
Flex the knee through available range, allowing the hip to flex with it
Read the angle at the end of available range
items.explanation: Position, fulcrum, alignment, motion, measurement. Allowing hip flexion matters: restricting it puts rectus femoris on stretch and will under-read knee flexion in a two-joint muscle. Record whether the measurement was active or passive, and be consistent between visits — mixing the two is a common source of apparent 'progress'.
items.citation: Norkin CC, White DJ. Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry. 5th ed. F.A. Davis; 2016 (knee flexion procedure).

items.stem: A patient presents within a day of a knee injury. Order the steps for applying the Ottawa Knee Rule.
orderedOptions: Confirm the rule applies: acute knee trauma, not an isolated superficial wound or a re-assessment of a known fracture
Ask the patient's age and check whether they are 55 or older
Palpate for isolated tenderness of the patella and for tenderness at the head of the fibula
Test whether the patient can flex the knee to 90 degrees
Ask the patient to take four weight-bearing steps, both immediately after injury and now
Refer for radiography if any one criterion is met; if none are met, imaging is not indicated
items.explanation: The five criteria are age 55 or over, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, and inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and at assessment. ANY single positive triggers imaging. The rule is designed to be over-inclusive — it exists to safely rule fracture OUT, not to predict who has one.
items.pearl: The Ottawa rules are a rule-out tool. A positive doesn't mean fracture; it means you can't skip the X-ray.
items.citation: Stiell IG, Greenberg GH, Wells GA, et al. Prospective validation of a decision rule for the use of radiography in acute knee injuries. JAMA. 1996;275(8):611-615; pooled accuracy per Bachmann LM, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2004;140(2):121-124.

items.stem: Benjaminse et al.'s meta-analysis reported the Lachman test at pooled sensitivity 85% and specificity 94% for ACL rupture. What does that profile support?
options: It is the single most useful stand-alone test — reasonably good at both ruling in and ruling out
It should only be used to confirm a tear, never to exclude one
It is a screening test with too many false positives to act on
It is unreliable and should be replaced by the anterior drawer
items.explanation: Sensitivity 85% with specificity 94% is an unusually balanced profile for an orthopaedic special test — most are good at one job only. That is why the Lachman is the recommended first-line clinical test for ACL rupture. It still misses roughly 1 in 7, so a convincing mechanism and haemarthrosis should keep the diagnosis alive despite a negative test.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. Clinical diagnosis of an anterior cruciate ligament rupture: a meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288.

items.stem: The pivot shift test has pooled sensitivity of about 24% and specificity of about 98% for ACL rupture. How should it be used?
options: As a confirmatory test — a positive is close to diagnostic, but a negative excludes nothing
As the primary screening test in the acute knee
Instead of the Lachman, since it is more specific
Only under anaesthesia, as it is meaningless awake
items.explanation: Specificity near 98% means false positives are rare, so a genuine pivot shift is strong evidence of ACL rupture — but sensitivity of 24% means roughly three in four ruptures do not show one in the clinic, largely because it is uncomfortable and guarding suppresses it. Sensitivity rises markedly under anaesthesia, which is a reminder that the same test performs differently depending on the conditions.
items.pearl: Lachman to screen, pivot shift to confirm. They are a pair, not alternatives.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288.

items.stem: The same meta-analysis found the anterior drawer performed well in CHRONIC ACL deficiency (about Sn 92% / Sp 91%) but poorly in ACUTE injuries. What explains the difference?
options: Acute haemarthrosis and hamstring guarding block the anterior translation the test depends on
The ligament heals enough within days to change the test result
Chronic tears are larger and therefore easier to detect
The test is performed at a different angle in chronic cases
items.explanation: At 90° of flexion the hamstrings are well positioned to resist anterior translation, and a painful, swollen acute knee guards hard. Weeks later, with the effusion settled and pain reduced, that same test becomes informative. The practical consequence: in the acutely injured knee, trust the Lachman, and re-examine once the joint has settled.
items.pearl: A negative examination in a hot, swollen, guarded knee is a weak negative. Re-examine at 5-7 days.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288.

items.stem: A meta-analysis of over 4,000 patients found the Ottawa Knee Rule had sensitivity around 98.5% and specificity around 49% for clinically significant knee fracture. What does the low specificity mean in practice?
options: Roughly half of patients without a fracture will still meet a criterion and be sent for imaging — the trade accepted to avoid missing fractures
The rule is too inaccurate to use
About half of fractures will be missed
The rule should only be applied to patients over 55
items.explanation: This is a deliberately asymmetric design. Near-perfect sensitivity means almost no significant fracture is missed, which is what a rule-out tool must achieve. The cost is a lot of negative X-rays. Even so, applying the rule reduces radiography substantially compared with imaging everyone — the point is fewer films, not zero films.
items.citation: Bachmann LM, Haberzeth S, Steurer J, ter Riet G. The accuracy of the Ottawa knee rule to rule out knee fractures: a systematic review. Ann Intern Med. 2004;140(2):121-124.

items.stem: A meta-analysis of meniscal special tests reported McMurray around Sn 61% / Sp 84%, joint-line tenderness around Sn 83% / Sp 83%, and Thessaly 20° around Sn 75% / Sp 87%. What is the honest summary?
options: No single meniscal test is accurate enough to rule a tear in or out on its own
Joint-line tenderness is sensitive enough to be used as a stand-alone rule-out test
Thessaly is accurate enough to replace MRI
McMurray is the most accurate of the three
items.explanation: All three sit in the middling range where likelihood ratios are too close to 1 to shift probability much. The review's authors were explicit that study quality was generally poor and heterogeneity high, so even these numbers should be held loosely. History — mechanism, locking, effusion timing — carries at least as much weight as any of these manoeuvres.
items.citation: Smith BE, Thacker D, Crewesmith A, Hall M. Special tests for assessing meniscal tears within the knee: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evid Based Med. 2015;20(3):88-97.
items.contestedNote: Reported accuracy for meniscal tests varies widely across studies, and this meta-analysis explicitly flags poor methodological quality and high heterogeneity. Earlier single studies (notably the original Thessaly report) gave far higher figures that independent work has not reproduced.

items.stem: In the same review, requiring BOTH the Thessaly and McMurray tests to be positive gave sensitivity around 53% and specificity around 62% — worse than either test alone. What is the lesson?
options: Combining tests does not automatically improve accuracy; a combination has to be validated as a combination
Test combinations always outperform single tests
It proves both tests are worthless
It means the tests should be performed in the opposite order
items.explanation: Clinicians often assume stacking tests must sharpen the picture. Requiring two positives should raise specificity and drop sensitivity — here specificity fell too, because the tests are not independent and the underlying data were weak. Validated clusters (like the Park cluster at the shoulder or the Flynn rule in the lumbar spine) earn their likelihood ratios empirically; ad hoc combinations do not inherit them.
items.pearl: You cannot compute a cluster's accuracy by multiplying its parts. Clusters must be studied as clusters.
items.citation: Smith BE, Thacker D, Crewesmith A, Hall M. Evid Based Med. 2015;20(3):88-97.

items.stem: A footballer felt a pop during a cutting movement, the knee swelled within an hour, and they could not continue. The Lachman is negative, but the knee is painful and guarded. Interpretation?
options: The negative lowers the probability but doesn't clear it — with this history, re-examine when the knee settles
ACL rupture is excluded; reassure and discharge
The result is meaningless because the patient is guarding
Proceed straight to surgical referral regardless
items.explanation: LR− around 0.16 is a genuinely useful negative in ideal conditions, but this is not ideal conditions: an immediate haemarthrosis with a pop and inability to continue is a high pretest probability, and guarding degrades the test. High pretest plus a compromised examination equals a probability that has NOT fallen enough to discharge. Re-examine at 5-7 days, and image if suspicion persists.
items.pearl: Rapid haemarthrosis after a pivoting injury is roughly a coin-flip for ACL rupture before you touch the knee. Weight the history accordingly.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288 (LR− computed from pooled Sn/Sp).

items.stem: Six weeks after a twisting injury, a patient reports the knee 'giving way' on turning. You elicit a clear pivot shift. What follows?
options: Strongly supports ACL rupture with rotatory instability — structure rehabilitation and onward discussion around it
A single positive test is never enough to act on
This confirms a meniscal tear
It rules out associated injuries
items.explanation: Specificity around 98% gives a positive likelihood ratio in double figures — from a moderate pretest probability this lands you in high-confidence territory. Combined with a history of giving way on rotation, this is the clinical picture of functional rotatory instability. It does not, however, exclude concomitant meniscal or chondral injury, which are common in this population.
items.citation: Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, van der Schans CP. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2006;36(5):267-288 (LR+ computed from pooled Sn/Sp).

items.stem: A 32-year-old twisted their knee yesterday. They are under 55, have no patellar or fibular head tenderness, can flex past 90°, and walked four steps both at the time and now. What does the Ottawa Knee Rule support?
options: Radiography is not indicated — the rule's near-perfect sensitivity makes a significant fracture very unlikely
Radiography is still required because of the mechanism
The rule cannot be applied within 24 hours of injury
A negative rule also excludes ligament and meniscal injury
items.explanation: All five criteria negative is exactly the situation the rule was built for: sensitivity near 98-100% means a clinically significant fracture is very unlikely, and imaging can be safely omitted. Crucially it says nothing about soft tissue — this patient may still have an ACL or meniscal injury, and the rest of your examination is unchanged.
items.pearl: Ottawa clears bone, not ligament. A negative rule is not a normal knee.
items.citation: Stiell IG, Greenberg GH, Wells GA, et al. JAMA. 1996;275(8):611-615; Bachmann LM, et al. Ann Intern Med. 2004;140(2):121-124.

items.stem: A 52-year-old has medial joint-line tenderness and a positive McMurray, with no trauma and gradual onset over months. MRI would likely show a degenerative meniscal tear. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: A degenerative meniscal finding is common at this age and may be incidental — treat the presentation, not the image
The positive tests confirm the meniscus is the pain source and surgery should be discussed
Meniscal tests are invalid over the age of 50
The absence of trauma rules out meniscal pathology
items.explanation: Degenerative meniscal tears are highly prevalent in middle-aged and older knees, including in people with no pain at all, and frequently coexist with early osteoarthritis. So a positive test plus a positive scan does not establish causation. Current evidence favours exercise-based management over arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears without true mechanical locking.
items.pearl: In the over-50 knee, 'meniscal tear on MRI' is often a finding, not a diagnosis.
items.citation: Englund M, Guermazi A, Gale D, et al. Incidental meniscal findings on knee MRI in middle-aged and elderly persons. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(11):1108-1115.

items.stem: You suspect patellofemoral pain. Which statement best reflects how the diagnosis is currently made?
options: It is a clinical diagnosis based on reproducing anterior knee pain with loaded knee flexion, after excluding other sources — no single special test establishes it
A positive patellar grind test confirms the diagnosis
MRI showing cartilage change is required
A positive patellar apprehension test is diagnostic
items.explanation: Current guidance defines patellofemoral pain by reproduction of retropatellar or peri-patellar pain during activities that load the flexed knee — squatting, stairs, running, prolonged sitting — with other diagnoses excluded. The classic palpation and compression tests have poor diagnostic properties. Patellar apprehension addresses instability, which is a different problem.
items.pearl: Patellofemoral pain is diagnosed by what provokes it, not by a manoeuvre you perform.
items.citation: Willy RW, Hoglund LT, Barton CJ, et al. Patellofemoral pain: clinical practice guidelines. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2019;49(9):CPG1-CPG95.

items.stem: A 58-year-old has activity-related knee pain, morning stiffness lasting about 15 minutes, and crepitus, with no red flags. What does current guidance support?
options: Knee osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically without imaging in this presentation
Radiographs are required before the diagnosis can be made
Morning stiffness of any duration points to inflammatory arthritis
MRI is needed to grade severity before starting treatment
items.explanation: Guidelines support a clinical diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis in a patient aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or morning stiffness lasting no longer than about 30 minutes. Imaging adds little for typical presentations and correlates poorly with symptoms. Prolonged morning stiffness, or systemic and inflammatory features, is what should redirect you.
items.pearl: Radiographic severity and symptom severity track each other poorly. Treat the person's function, not the film.
items.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG226; 2022.

items.stem: Published MCID values for the KOOS subscales differ substantially between populations — for example roughly 10-16 points after tibial tubercle osteotomy versus roughly 12-27 points after ACL reconstruction. How should this be handled?
options: Quote the MCID for a population resembling your patient, and treat it as a band rather than a threshold
Use the lowest published value so improvement is easier to demonstrate
Use a single average across all populations
Abandon the KOOS in favour of a single-item pain score
items.explanation: The MCID is a property of the measure plus the population, the intervention, the baseline severity, and the anchor used. A value derived after ACL reconstruction in young athletes does not transfer to a post-osteotomy or osteoarthritic population. Different KOOS subscales also carry different thresholds — sport and quality of life typically need larger changes than pain or activities of daily living.
items.citation: Retzky JS, et al. Defining the minimal clinically important difference for IKDC and KOOS scores for patients undergoing tibial tubercle osteotomy. J Exp Orthop. 2024;11(3):e12115; ACL reconstruction thresholds per time-to-achievement analysis, Am J Sports Med. 2021.
items.contestedNote: KOOS MCID estimates vary widely by subscale, population, and procedure (roughly 10 to 27 points across the studies cited). No single value is authoritative.

items.stem: A patient's IKDC Subjective Knee Form score improves by 5 points over six weeks, against reported MCID values of roughly 8-9 points in comparable populations. What can you conclude?
options: The change is below the reported threshold — not yet demonstrably meaningful, though it may be early
The patient has meaningfully improved
The patient has deteriorated
The IKDC is not valid for tracking change
items.explanation: Five points falls short of the commonly reported 8-9 point threshold, so this does not yet clear the bar for a change patients notice. That is not the same as failure: six weeks may simply be early, and the score may be missing gains in the specific activities this person cares about. Pair it with a patient-nominated measure and re-check.
items.citation: IKDC MCID values around 8.5-8.6 points reported in knee osteoarthritis and tibial tubercle osteotomy populations; see Retzky JS, et al. J Exp Orthop. 2024;11(3):e12115.
items.contestedNote: IKDC MCID estimates cluster around 8-9 points in the populations cited but vary with condition and timepoint; treat as approximate.

items.stem: Roughly what is the expected normal adult range of knee flexion measured by goniometry?
options: About 135 degrees
About 90 degrees
About 160 degrees
About 110 degrees
items.explanation: Standard adult norms put knee flexion at approximately 135 degrees, with extension to 0. Functional demands sit well below full range for most activities — level walking needs roughly 60 degrees, stairs more, and deep squatting or kneeling considerably more — so the functional target should be set by the patient's actual demands rather than by the textbook number.
items.pearl: Compare with the other knee before comparing with a table. Individual variation is wide.
items.citation: Norkin CC, White DJ. Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry. 5th ed. F.A. Davis; 2016 (AAOS normative values, knee flexion).

items.stem: When judging readiness to return to pivoting sport after ACL reconstruction, which combination best reflects current evidence?
options: Time since surgery AND objective strength and hop symmetry — both, not either alone
Time since surgery alone, once nine months have passed
Quadriceps strength symmetry alone, whenever achieved
Patient confidence alone, since fear is the main barrier
items.explanation: Evidence supports delaying return to pivoting sport and requiring objective symmetry — quadriceps strength and hop test performance — rather than relying on either the calendar or a single test. Reinjury risk falls substantially when both are satisfied. Psychological readiness is a genuine additional factor, not a substitute for physical criteria.
items.pearl: Passing criteria late beats passing them early. Time and symmetry both independently predict reinjury.
items.citation: Grindem H, Snyder-Mackler L, Moksnes H, Engebretsen L, Risberg MA. Simple decision rules can reduce reinjury risk by 84% after ACL reconstruction: the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort study. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50(13):804-808.

items.stem: You want to know whether a patient can now kneel to lay flooring — the specific task that stopped them working. Which measure answers that most directly?
options: Patient-Specific Functional Scale, with 'kneeling to lay flooring' nominated as an activity
KOOS
Numeric Pain Rating Scale
Goniometric knee flexion
items.explanation: Each answers a different question. The PSFS tracks activities the patient nominates, so it maps exactly onto this goal. The KOOS gives standardised, comparable domains; the NPRS measures pain intensity; goniometry measures an impairment that may or may not be the limiting factor. Knee flexion range is necessary for kneeling but far from sufficient — pain, confidence, and tolerance all matter.
items.citation: Horn KK, Jennings S, Richardson G, et al. The Patient-Specific Functional Scale: psychometrics, clinimetrics, and application as a clinical outcome measure. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2012;42(1):30-42.
